newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline, platinum and palladium prices soar.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline, platinum and palladium prices soar.

text.p: Gasoline prices rose sharply on Friday as refinery disruptions in Europe were expected to detain cargoes of gasoline scheduled to supply the United States in the next few weeks.

In other markets, platinum and palladium prices soared on fresh worries about supply problems in Russia and South Africa, and corn prices ended mostly higher as traders worried that rains will miss the stressed Midwest crop this weekend.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline for September delivery closed 2.27 cents a gallon higher at 65.07 cents and set a life-of-contract high during the day.

"Gasoline supplies are of the utmost concern right now. Implied demand is running more than 8.5 million barrels per day while production is less than eight million, so we have been depending on imports to close the gap," said Richard Redash, analyst with Prudential Securities in New York.
"Given the refinery problems in Europe and the tight supply/demand balance, I think this is a correct response," said Redash.

An official of Nerefco, a British Petroleum/Texaco joint venture in Rotterdam, said a 55,000 barrel per day catalytic cracker at its refinery was shut on Friday and would rem,ain closed "for a few days" because of production problems.

Meanwhile, the 60,000 barrel per day Coryton catalytic cracker in the United Kingdom operated by British Petroelum and Mobil Corp was also shut down for "essential maintenance following technical problems," a BP spokesman said.

Traders said that with such near-term uncertainty about gasoline, the oil complex ignored the expected resumption of Iraqi oil sales that has been looming over the market and grudgingly tracked gasoline higher.
September crude oil ended 14 cents a barrel higher at $20.28 and September heating oil 0.37 cent a gallon higher at 56.56 cents.
Platinum and palladium prices soared on Friday amid worries about supplies from Russia drying up again and additional supply shortages if South African miners strike.
September palladium at the NYMEX jumped the $6 allowable daily trading limit from the opening bell and stayed their all day, closing at $206.60 an ounce, a new contract high.
Spot palladium ended quoted $224.60/227.60 an ounce, the highest levels since a 17-year high near $240.00 in June.
Platinum of October delivery gained $13.00 to end at $438.50 an ounce after also setting a a new contract high.

No further Russian shipments of platinum group metals are expected in Japan under the annual supply contract until at least August 6, traders said. Offerings earlier this week by Russia in the spot market of parcels of only about 15,000 ounces of platinum were not meeting demand, they added.

"The exact size of the shipment (to Japan) is not yet known, and Japan has almost completely run out of supplies of platinum," analyst Richard Harrison of brokers T. Hoare & Co said in a weekly report.
Russian exports of platinum and palladium resumed in July after a six months suspension. Russia supplies about 20 percent of the world's platinum and 60 percent of its palladium.
Meanwhile, South Africa's Impala Platinum Holdings Ltd said all workers at its platinum refineries had reported for work desite a National Union of Mineworkers notice of a strike on Thursday.
The NUM said later Friday that the strike had been put on hold while the South African Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration considered the wage dispute.
Impala produced 499,000 ounces of platinum in the second half of 1996. South Africa produces about 60 pct of world platinum and Impala about a third of South Africa's output.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn prices eked out gains late as traders battled with differing views of how dryness and heat in the Midwest was affecting the pollinating crop.
September corn ended 3 cents a bushel higher at $2.68-1/2.
Weather forecasts at midday suggested a few scattered showers could reach central Illinois and Indiana this weekend.

"I think the day was marked by a little bit more uncertainty," John Kleist, president of the Commodity Advisory Group at Sagamore Partners, said. "There were some hints of moisture showing up in the central and southern Corn Belt."
But traders said the weekend's weather will be critical to crop conditions as signs of moisture stress were already visible in Missouri, Illinois and Indiana.

"I can't believe that we haven't lost a fairly substantial portion of the corn yield," said William Wiebold, agronomist at the University of Missouri. "The leaves are rolled and are actually sunburned. The tissue is actually turning gray and has been damaged because it has been so hot and dry."
